Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the
Minister of Finance regarding the action of Noranda Mines Limited in substantially hiking the price of copper despite the fact that its profit position this year improved by some 6 per cent over last year. I should like to ask the minister two questions. First, does he consider this move to be inflationary in contravention of the restraints he asked all parts of the economy to observe? Second, what action, if any, does the government intend to take?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I suggest to the hon. member that in respect of the first part of his question he is asking for an expression of opinion from the minister. The second part of the question would appear to be in order.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday I was made aware of the reported increase in the price of copper by the Noranda mine. I was a little astonished to read in the Globe and Mail this morning an article dealing with this move on the part of the company in which the following appeared:
This is an inflationary world; if the government will stop spending so much we could help to keep the price of copper down-
The reason I take exception to this statement is that I understand the Noranda company is going to tie in the price of copper with prices in the United States and not in Canada. I can assure the hon. gentleman that I intend to investigate the situation.

I have a supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. I wish to thank the minister for the answer he has given and ask him whether, following the investigation, the government will make public the results of his inquiries as to whether this increase is justified in the light of the company's favourable profit position.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I shall be prepared to answer further questions.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the Minister of Finance whether he can indicate to the house the extent of Canada's contribution to the support being given Great Britain through the I.M.F.?
November 21, 1967

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO CANADIAN CONTRIBUTION TO U.K. SUPPORT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I calculated that under the I.M.F. arrangement the Canadian contribution in various forms would be approximately $91 million. In addition there will be an arrangement among the central banks and we will be taking a proportionate share of the total obligation. It has not been customary to reveal these obligations of the central banks, and I hope I will not be pressed on the matter. We are taking our proportionate share of the total support being given.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO CANADIAN CONTRIBUTION TO U.K. SUPPORT
speechtext: Is that support in the form of an outright advance or a credit which can be drawn on from time to time?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO CANADIAN CONTRIBUTION TO U.K. SUPPORT
speechtext: In the case of the I.M.F. of course, resources would be made available to the United Kingdom government to be called upon from time to time as required. This would take the form of part of the gold in the I.M.F. and other forms of quotas we have subscribed. In the case of the arrangement among the central banks, this would be in the form of a stand-by to show the massive support behind the present rate of the United Kingdom pound sterling.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: POSSIBLE EFFECT OF DEVALUATION ON CANADIAN GRAIN PRICES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, perhaps my question should be directed to the Minister of Trade and Commerce but in his absence I will direct it to the Minister of Finance with the hope that he can provide an answer. Is the minister in a position to indicate what effect the devaluation of the pound will have on the price Canadian farmers will receive for their wheat, particularly in relation to the Chinese wheat agreement, since payments by the Chinese are made in sterling?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: POSSIBLE EFFECT OF DEVALUATION ON CANADIAN GRAIN PRICES
speechtext:
I do not expect it will have any effect, Mr. Speaker. These transactions with China are made in sterling but they are hedged, and I do not think there is any reason to expect
Inquiries of the Ministry that the western farmer will suffer on the Chinese market as a result of the devaluation of sterling.

maintopic: POSSIBLE EFFECT OF DEVALUATION ON CANADIAN GRAIN PRICES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in view of the fact that flax will now cost the British 50 cents a bushel more and wheat will cost 28 cents a bushel more, will the minister acting on behalf of the Minister of Trade and Commerce contact the wheat board to determine whether a conference is now taking place between representatives of the wheat board and Great Britain in order to assure that Great Britain will continue to purchase our wheat and flax at those levels?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: POSSIBLE EFFECT OF DEVALUATION ON CANADIAN GRAIN PRICES
speechtext: As the hon. gentleman knows, the wheat board and the British mills are in almost continuous consultation. There would be no need to call a special conference for this purpose. I expect our wheat will remain just as competitive in the British market as it has been hitherto in relation to United States, Argentine or other varieties of wheat. I do not think there is any reason to anticipate either lower prices or smaller sales as a result of devaluation.

maintopic: POSSIBLE EFFECT OF DEVALUATION ON CANADIAN GRAIN PRICES
speechtext: A further supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. Could the minister assure the house that there is a contract with Canada under which Great Britain will continue to purchase our wheat at this time?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: POSSIBLE EFFECT OF DEVALUATION ON CANADIAN GRAIN PRICES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, there are contracts between the British mills and the wheat board. The British government does not buy wheat; I think the hon. gentleman should know that. He is a good western member, has been for a number of years, and I should think over the years he should have absorbed something about wheat trading. In any event, our contracts are being fulfilled. Our sales to Britain are made in dollars, of course, and not in sterling.

maintopic: POSSIBLE EFFECT OF DEVALUATION ON CANADIAN GRAIN PRICES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, earlier the Minister of Finance indicated that the price the farmers will receive for their wheat will not be affected because of hedging. I wonder if the minister can say now that this hedging will cover all future sales including the negotiations now under way with China?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: POSSIBLE EFFECT OF DEVALUATION ON CANADIAN GRAIN PRICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I can only say that this is the policy of the Canadian Wheat Board.

speakeroldname: Mr. John R. Malheson (Parliamentary Secretary to Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Leader of the Opposition in his maiden speech charges economic mismanagement. Indeed, he was sorely tempted, he said, to substitute the words "rotten management". Does his charge have substance? I believe it does not.
Let me present, Mr. Speaker, some representative views of our economic progress. I should like to refer to the newsletter of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce dated January, 1967, which makes reference to the fact that in 1966 Canada's national output in real terms rose by 6 per cent to 7 per cent over 1965. It was confirmed that total employment increased more in 1966 than in any previous post-war year.
According to "Canadian Farm Economics" for February, 1967 the economy is now effectively fully employed and cannot readily draw on slack resources for expansion. On the basis of this the conclusion is reached that a more moderate rate of real growth in 1967 than in the previous year is indicated.
If I may refer to the Globe and Mail for July 4, 1967 there is a lead article dealing with the economic forecasters of the govern-
Suggested Economic Mismanagement ment of Ontario. The headline is "Ontario expects 7 per cent more growth this year; optimistic about 1968."
In the Financial Post for July 29, 1967, in an editorial headlined "The Nation's Business", it is stated there are fresh reasons now for confidence.
I should also like to quote the mid-year review of private and public investment in Canada prepared by the Dominion Bureau of Statistics under date of August, 1967. There we read:
The strengthening in investment plans has occurred in both the business and the housing and social capital sectors.
I should also like to refer to the cautious statement by the Minister of Finance in his remarks on the budget on October 4, 1967, which are to be found at page 2808 of Hansard. The Minister of Finance said:
-I would still expect the gross national product this year to increase by 7 per cent or a bit more-
The Toronto Telegram for October 11, 1967 reports the prediction of Mr. Donald B. Marsh of the Royal Bank of Canada. Under the heading "Our economy will expand at faster rate in 1968", Mr. Marsh predicts a 1968 gross national product-total value of goods and services sold-of 8Jt per cent to 9 per cent higher in value and 5 per cent higher in volume than in 1967.
Looking at the Vancouver Sun for October 13, 1967, I discover the encouraging prediction of Dr. Harry L. Purdy that the odds are ten to one against recession. The Winnipeg Free Press for October 31 reports part of the speech of the newly appointed chairman of the Economic Council of Canada, Dr. Arthur J. R. Smith, in regard to the possibilities of economic growth in the years ahead. According to this gentleman we can look forward for many years to rapidly expanding economic potentials, "to future potentials of truly extraordinary dimensions".
These are, I submit, representative views of informed Canadians about the conditions we are now facing, Mr. Speaker. Professor Harry G. Johnson, speaking to the Canadian Club of Toronto on November 5, 1962. discussed the long run problem of slow economic growth. His topic was "Canada in a changing world". Remember, Mr. Speaker, the year was 1962. Professor Johnson said:
The two real problems have been and remain foreign competition-specifically European and Japanese competition-and domestic stagnation. These two problems are obviously interrelated. I interpret them basically as manifestations of a fundamental trend in the world economy, a trend sure to continue-the spread of industrialization.
November 21, 1967

Suggested Economic Mismanagement
In that address he described the post-war industrial revolution which has occurred in Europe, the oil, electricity, chemicals and plastics revolution, and the industrialization of underdeveloped nations, most apparent in the rapid emergence of Japan as an advanced industrial country. The question as I see it now is, do we really wish to enter the big league of progress or simply fade into the obscurity of a new phase of North American opulence, laziness, and then decadence? I am all for getting out into the world whatever may be the risks.
Even more, I believe right now that if we have the will we can be unique builders in Asia and in Europe. We as no other country could start the movement to cause anxious mankind to work together for good. I rejoice that the Prime Minister is in London today. I hope while we still have him at the helm he will visit several world capitals for serious policy discussions. No man that Canada has produced more truly epitomizes faith and hope and charity. This great human personality whom each of us knows as a parliamentary colleague and friend should not be wasted.
No, Mr. Speaker, this is not a time of despair but rather a time of challenge and opportunity. The great work of this centennial parliament is not ended; it is coming at last to its full fruition. We rejoice that the new Leader of the Opposition has joined us to share in its glory.
I wonder whether the hon. member would permit a question?
Of course.

The hon. member mentioned the Prime Minister and said "so long as we have him at the helm...". Would he give an indication to the house how long this is going to be, because he seems to have some doubt about the Prime Minister continuing.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have never heard of any prime minister continuing indefinitely, but I think we are particularly favoured in Canada in having this great world citizen heading Canadian affairs at this momentous time. I hope his great talents will be used to the full. I can think of no respect in which he could serve Canada more now than by making visits to important centres of the world to hold high level discussions with influential world personalities.

That was not my question.

[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)

Mr. Speaker, yesterday afternoon, the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) moved here in this House of Commons a non-confidence motion reading as follows:
This house regrets that the mismanagement of this government has endangered the rate of economic growth, the prospects of satisfactory levels of employment, and the ability of individual Canadians to meet their own commitments.
Mr. Speaker, I had the privilege of seconding that motion. In fact, I was convinced that the Canadian people have lost confidence in this government and that it was the duty of any member to take all the means available to overthrow the government. I agree with the Leader of the Opposition that it is our patriotic duty to overthrow this government as soon as possible.
I am convinced also, on the basis of conversations with my constituents, that the citizens of Canada, in general, agree with us and share our desire to see another government replace this incompetent, weak and wretched government.
A few minutes ago I heard the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Matheson) say that several people were congratulating the government and that others had faith in the future of Canada.
We also have faith in the future of Canada. We are convinced that a great future is in store for Canada, but we do not share with the hon. member for Leeds the opinion that the present government is able to manage the affairs our country, as it thinks it can.
In his speech yesterday, the Leader of the opposition gave several reasons why the Canadian people have lost confidence in the present government. I shall not repeat all the reasons for which they have lost their confidence in the government, but I should still like to mention a few which serve as a basis for speaking as I do.
First of all, the Canadian people are not gullible, they can make allowances. Canadians have drawn a parallel between the actions and the words of the present government, and they have realized, without too much trouble, that there is quite a margin between the words and the acts of the Pearson government.
The people also know that promises have been made during election campaigns only as a lure for Canadians and in order to get votes.
November 21. 1967	COMMONS DEBATES
That is why today, having seen the actions of the government which had promised a sort of paradise on earth, the Canadian people have come to the conclusion that the government no longer deserves their confidence.
Mr. Speaker, may I recall, for example, some of the promises which were forgotten as soon as they were made.
At the top of the list, to mention only a few, there is the post of Minister of Agriculture for eastern Canada which, I repeat, was promised during the 1963 and 1965 election campaigns and which has never been created.
The 10,000 scholariships promised to students have also never been granted.
The 7 per cent bonus for bilingual civil servants has not been paid as promised. Our secretaries, who are bilingual, are still waiting for the 7 per cent bonus which the Liberal government had promised to give bilingual civil servants. This is another promise which has not been fulfilled. If my information is correct, the reason why the secretaries of members of parliament have not received this 7 per cent bonus is that a senior member of the cabinet objects strenuously to these secretaries, whose services the members find so useful, being given what was promised them.
Medicare which had been promised for July 1, 1967, was put off a first time, and I would not be at all surprised-even if we were categorically promised today that the plan will come into force on July 1, 1968-if it were shelved once again.
Some time ago, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) had made us aware of the fact that the department wanted to reduce expenditures. Well, if we look at the facts as they are, we can only note that not only are government expenditures continuing at the same rate but that, in some cases, they are increasing.
Everyone also knows, Mr. Speaker, that even within the cabinet there are conflicts and disagreements now that filter through to the public.
Those are the reasons which have led the Canadian people to lose confidence in this government.
Another promise was made by our friends opposite, namely full employment. However they never fulfilled that promise, because in the Montreal and Quebec areas, we are now experiencing a rather alarming rate of unemployment.
Suggested Economic Mismanagement
I remember, Mr. Speaker, in what circumstances our friends opposite came into power in 1963. They went across the country instilling doubt and fear in the minds of people, launching a denigration campaign on the solvency of Canada and stating that the devaluation of the dollar would lead Canada to bankruptcy.
We have evidence of their sincerity, since after four years in office, they took great care not to reinstate the dollar to its former value.
As I said a moment ago, the thing that mattered in 1963 and in 1965 was to gain votes, and all means were good for that.
It is fitting also to recall that our friends opposite had left us, in 1958, a very poor legacy. We inherited unemployment, while in 1963, our country was in a prosperous economic situation. Through daring measures, through the continuous and strenuous work of the then ministers we had given new impetus to our economy.
All our friends opposite had to do was to follow the road we had mapped out for them. They did just that and that is why, if we enjoy today a degree of progress, we owe it to legislation passed and implemented by the previous government.
Mr. Speaker, I said that unemployment in the province of Quebec is a disquieting problem. I am not the only one to stress that situation because barely a few weeks ago the chairman of the executive council of the city of Montreal, Mr. Lucien Saulnier, sounded a warning and thus tried to get the support and co-operation of the government to undertake or continue works which would have created jobs and alleviated unemployment.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
On a few occasions I have myself asked in this house whether the government would be ready to make a financial contribution with a view to extending the subway. The amazing thing is that even though the Prime Minister is aware of the present unemployment, his answer was very brief, but to the point. It was a flat refusal.
I renewed my request a few days later and asked the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Marchand) whether he would not take the necessary steps, meet with the chairman of the executive committee in an attempt to come to an agreement and find a way to provide jobs for the unemployed in Montreal. His answer was also quite clear: If
4512	COMMONS
Suggested Economic Mismanagement Mr. Saulnier has anything to discuss with me, he is always welcome.
These are very definite answers I admit, answers that are slightly tinted with arrogance and almost show unconcern by our friends opposite over a solution to the unemployment problem.
It is known that by mid-October 1967, 4.7 per cent of the labour force was unemployed in the province of Quebec compared to 4.1 per cent in September 1967, 3.7 in 1966 and 2.4 in 1965. This is indicative of the increased unemployment in the province of Quebec.
On November 13 last, more than 4,000 railroad employees were unemployed. I would not be surprised if this number had increased since, and we would be justified in suggesting that this large number of unemployed is due to the poor management of the Department of Transport which has increased freight rates too markedly.
Another fact which causes concern is that, compared to last September, there are 42,000 fewer jobs in October. This year, 33,000 employees in the construction industry, 12,000 in the Montreal area, have lost their job and 18,000 jobs have also been lost in the manufacturing industry.
Since 1966, the number of workers has gone up by 172,000 whereas the number of new jobs has increased by only 113,000. That is very disturbing to the people who are concerned with the well-being of those who must go to work every day to earn their living.
But it does not seem to concern unduly the members of the cabinet because, at different times, I asked them, as did many other members, what means the government intended to take to create new jobs with a view to helping the unemployed in the province of Quebec in particular, and throughout Canada as a whole. We were always told that this would come in due course, without being given any other details.
In fact, Mr. Speaker, I think that the government does not have any plan ready and one fine day, we shall wake up as we did in 1956, in the midst of a depression and unprecedented unemployment, although our hon. friends opposite will have been warned, as they were in 1956, by the economists.
Mr. Speaker, I would still have many things to mention and discuss, but since others have also things to say and suggestions to make, I shall be brief. However, I should like to recall that during the sixties, there were,

on this side of the house, some Liberal members who claimed that they had the solutions and the answers to all questions.
I still recall, Mr. Speaker, the speeches made then by the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) and Messrs. Chevrier and Pickersgill, former members for Laurier and Bonavista-Twillingate.
Not one day would go by, Mr. Speaker, without those three hon. members making a concerted attack on the government, scrutinizing every lay-off they could find across the country, with the result that they spread panic in the people's minds.
I recall hearing at that time, in this house, Mr. Chevrier, the former minister, give a list of 25 different projects that, if implemented, he thought would remove unemployment overnight and benefit the Canadian people as a whole.
In closing, I would like to ask my friends opposite to rummage in their old bag of tricks, their old files from the time they were in opposition, and to resurrect those wonderful projects. If they were sincere at the time, Mr. Speaker, they should put their sincerity to the test today for the benefit of the labour force in this country.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure all hon. members are pleased to have heard the first speech made by the hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) in the house. Canadians generally and members of parliament in particular are keenly interested in the viewpoints of the hon. gentleman since, as hon. members well know, there has been a lot of talk throughout the country and in the press that there is a new look within the Conservative party.
Yesterday afternoon I listened intently when the hon. gentleman was making his speech and I also read his speech very carefully this morning to see if it was possible to find out what new direction, what new philosophy and new purposes the official opposition now had as a result of the change in the leadership of their party. It was a rather fruitless exercise, Mr. Speaker, because there was not very much that was very interesting in the speech he made yesterday. I thought that when I read it perhaps it would be better than it seemed when I listened to it but, alas, the same result was apparent after reading the speech very carefully.

[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
I was interested in the remarks of the hon. gentleman when he referred to rule changes which ought to be made in the house, although they did not involve setting up new regulations as much as finding ways and means so that the House of Commons could expedite the business of the country at the national level. He seemed to be of the opinion that there should be a greater attempt to expedite the business by consensus rather than by rules and regulations so that we would have the kind of flexibility we ought to have in order to meet the contingencies which arise in the country and come before this house from time to time. I find myself in agreement with this contention. He also suggested that we should dust off the rules of relevancy and repetition. I suggest that here too is an area where we could possibly make some improvements so far as debates in this house are concerned. The hon. gentleman went on to suggest that there should be agreement between the parties as to timetables and that sort of thing.
I realize that the hon. gentleman has not been in the house for a long time and in case some of his own members have not told him I think I ought to mention that the government house leader has been trying to do this for months without any apparent co-operation or inclination to co-operate on the part of the official opposition.
That is not right.

It is all very well to use nice phrases about offering to co-operate and so on, but I am far more interested in the action that follows assertions of this kind. I am trying to draw the attention of the Canadian people to the kind of farce the house was exposed to yesterday afternoon because so far as I am concerned actions speak louder than words. No matter how fine-sounding the words may be, if there is no follow-up to give effect to those words they are so much superfluous rhetoric.
The hon. gentleman also mentioned, as reported in Hansard on page 4459, that he
November 21, 1967

I should like to say that I have no fear of allowing the government to proceed with its legislation.
Earlier he had said:
As I said before, we are in politics to help get things started, not to get them stopped.
Mr. Speaker, I say he has that all wrong, because so far as legislation is concerned it seems that, although the government introduces legislation, when the debate will stop so that we can vote on it is up to the opposition. So far as the broadcasting legislation is concerned we have seen what the new look of the Conservative party is. However, while the hon. gentleman was in fact the leader of the party at that time, he was not in the house. He could not take his seat, of course, until after the election on November 6. We do hope that now he is in the house and sitting on the front benches he will in fact give effect to these promises. I believe that those of us who have been here for quite a number of years, however, will wonder with some concern whether or not the party opposite is capable of discipline in cooperating with the government to get the business through the house.
I have given the record of performance in this regard so far as co-operation in the house is concerned. I should like now to speak about another matter or two raised by the Leader of the Opposition. He had quite a lot to say about such things as the loss of confidence in the government, in parliament, and so on, by the people of Canada. He had things to say, for example, about export markets. As reported on page 4462 of Hansard he said:
Certainly the degree of inflation which has taken place in this country in recent years has seriously undermined our ability to compete and our ability to move ahead at a satisfactory rate.
Then some hon. members said "Hear, hear." They were hon. members from the other side who have not done their homework because that statement is not in accordance with the facts.

speakeroldname: Mr. Muir (Cape Breton North and Victoria):
speechtext: Your thoughts do not mean very much in view of the mess the country is in.

If I might give some statistics, Canada's share of exports has been steadily

expanding. Our export growth has been a major expansionist force in advancing the Canadian economy. Canada's exports increased by 18 per cent from 1965 to 1966 and by a further 11 per cent from January to September, 1967, a period of nine months. For the whole calendar year exports are expected to reach $11J billion, up from $10-3 billion in 1966 and $8J billion in 1965. Thus, in the space of two years Canada's exports have grown by 28 per cent compared with the growth in world exports of 17 per cent. In fact, during this same period Canada's exports have risen faster than those of any other major trading nation. The hon. gentleman and his colleagues do not bother to look up the facts before making these statements. Canada's share of world exports has been expanding and presently comprise 5 per cent of total world trade compared with 4.6 per cent in 1965 and 4.4 per cent in 1963.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
A particularly notable feature of Canada's recent performance is the strong growth in sales to the United States. Yesterday the hon. gentleman complained about Canada's position relative to the United States, yet our exports into that market have been going up substantially faster than the movement the other way. In the past two year period Canada's sales to that market have grown by two fifths whereas United States total imports have grown by one quarter. Thus Canada's share of the United States import market has been expanding steadily.
There was a substantial increase in exports of automotive products and this contributed in an important way to the improved position in the United States market, but new gains have also been made in other categories. It is noteworthy that the sharpest gains in Canada's exports continue to be made in the highly competitive field of fully manufactured goods. That is one thing the hon. gentleman complained about.
What about wheat?

I will get around to that subject in a moment or two. If the hon. gentleman would like to look at an answer to a question I placed on the order paper some two or three weeks ago in respect of wheat he will find that since 1963 there has been a progressive improvement in the export sales of wheat and flour by Canada, unprecedented in the history of our participation in trade.

What about this year?

I will get around to that in a moment. I suggest to hon. gentlemen opposite that they should do this house and the people of Canada the courtesy of doing their homework by looking at the statistics before they come here and make misleading statements designed to create gloom and doom, which in my view is a disservice to Canada generally.
Mr. Speaker, would the hon. gentleman permit a question?
Well, all these interruptions really have no value because they are based on nothing.

I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member but I wanted to ask him a question about exports before he moves to another subject. Will the hon. member not agree that the great increase in Canada's exports is due to the devaluation of the dollar brought about in 1962?

There may have been some relevance in that regard, and I do not doubt that, but I was not talking about 1962, 1963, and 1964. I was talking about the tremendously significant expansion in exports in 1965, 1966 and 1967 when the initial impact of that devaluation must surely have passed.
I was talking also about exactly the same period to which the Leader of the Opposition directed his complaints, and that is what is relevant to this debate.
Before turning to another subject let me place a few statistics on the record so hon. gentlemen will not have so much trouble digging them up for themselves. I have before me a table indicating the percentage of exports of major trading nations. These percentage increases give a clear picture of the situation in 1966 compared with 1965. When we rose for the dinner recess I was discussing the shocking action of the Noranda company in raising the price of copper. In this connection I should like to quote from a statement made by Mr. James Thomas, vice president of Phillips Cables Limited of Brockville, who said:
The increase is definitely inflationary. The company is not a Noranda customer and will not be immediately affected, but the increase and subsequent additions will mean a 20 to 30 per cent increase in the cost of wire and cable.
This is inflation of the worst kind. This can affect the whole building industry. The economy cannot afford it.
This afternoon, when this particular situation was brought to the minister's attention, he said in somewhat vague terms that he intended to look into it and do something about it. I admit I am a little dubious about what he is likely to do, since this government has consistently rejected the proposal which this party has put forward for a long time for the setting up of a prices review board. It would be too lengthy a process to establish one to deal with this sort of situation. I believe it is time the minister considered something more effective than merely warning or pleading with these rapacious corporations to avoid adding to our economic difficulties; he should be consulting the provinces in which these companies are located and urging them to use their constitutional powers to establish price controls over these basic industries. Otherwise they will get completely out of hand.
The minister was quite satirical yesterday-at least he thought he was satirical- about the proposals made by the leader of this party with regard to the control of private industry. In this connection he made one of the cheapest and snidest comments ever made in the course of a cheap, snide and frivolous speech, when he said this:
I sometimes wonder, when I listen to such talk about having control over the private sector as well as the public sector, whether it does not really mean that the hon. gentleman's party would like to limit competition-to ensure that one of their friends would have an opportunity of building a shop somewhere and that competition in that area would be limited.
There, I think, is an example of the cheap, flippant, frivolous attitude of this Minister of Finance. He is apparently wholly ignorant of the fact that he is directing investment in Canada every day-and directing it very

badly-by way of unjustifiable and unjustified depreciation allowances which force our scarce capital into a certain sector of the economy, which ties us more closely to the United States market and renders us less able to manage our own affairs.
When we propose that there should be an investment board to enable the government to determine the direction of our economy and the investment which will decide that direction, the minister should take this more seriously than he does now. I say to him that he will encounter continued trouble unless he does something of this sort. I should like to spend a moment or two of the few that are left in pointing out how shocking it is that the government of a country like Canada can reduce it to the situation in which we find ourselves today-a country which has continually rising production, and enormous personal savings that rose by the end of the second quarter of this year to the phenomenal figure of $3,940,000,000. This, in addition to the retained earnings of the corporations, makes our constant plea that we require foreign capital, and require our ministers to go to New York and beg for it, highly suspect.
In this week's Financial Post the president of the Toronto chamber of commerce draws attention to the fact that Canada has now grown up and that we are ourselves a source of investment capital. He did not say where the capital goes, but I have been doing some analyses and have discovered just where it is going. I found that a very large part of it is going to the United States, and to pay for a rapidly rising volume of imports-$8,620 million in 1965, $10,102 million in 1966, and at the rate of $12 billion this year. We have been pouring money across the line in the form of interest, dividends and equity and portfolio investments. Much of this money has gone in the form of interest and dividends to the United States owners of equities and bonds, and there is not much we can do about that. But a large proportion of it represents the savings of Canadians which are being invested in the United States by those who have control of those savings-the various financial institutions of this country.
I say to the Minister of Finance that if he can bring himself to inquire, however reluctantly, into the activites of the chartered banks he could make some inquiries about the volume of Canadian savings which those banks are funnelling into the New York call market, enabling them to make an extremely

Mr. Speaker, my grievance today has to do with the laws and the making of laws in Canada, with particular reference to the law of expropriation. Before I proceed with that part of my grievance, I should like to say that I have always understood that Canada, as a democracy, is governed by laws that are made to provide the greatest good for the greatest number of citizens. After being a member of this parliament for almost ten years, I wonder how much attention parliament actually pays to democracy in making the laws to provide the greatest good to the greatest number? I think very little. A great many of our laws appear to be made with a view to political expediency and providing for the wishes of certain classes of people in our country and without any apparent regard for the well-being or interest of the greater number of people who may be concerned.
At times one appears to be justified in feeling like the character Mr. Bumble in one of Charles Dickens' works who remarked so aptly, "The law is a ass, a idiot". There are times, very many times, when one wonders if that is not perfectly true. Until I became a member of parliament almost ten years ago, I used to think that the laws were all made with a view to carrying out the democratic principles we are supposed to have in this country. However, since coming into a full understanding of the way some of the laws are forced on the country, without any regard at all for the feelings of the majority of Canadians, I have begun to wonder just where we are going.
An example of this is shown by the present government in the present debate on the emasculated capital punishment bill, under the provisions of which our nation is to be divided into first and second class citizens, so far as protection is concerned. If this bill on capital punishment is approved, then as I have already stated, God forbid, it will certainly divide us all into first and second class citizens. This is not the will, Mr. Speaker, of the majority of the people of Canada.

The second example is the bill that was finally passed on January 27, 1967 and which is now law. That was the bill to amend the Railway Act and to set up Mr. PickersgilTs empire, he now being chairman of the Canadian Transport Commission. That bill along with the Canadian National Railways Act and the Expropriation Act, gives the Canadian National Railways almost carte blanche to do anything it pleases, without reference to parliament or regard for the welfare of any people who may be involved or who get in the way of the ambitions of the railway, whatever they may be. Certainly the Canadian National Railways Act and the Expropriation Act taken together makes this sort of thing possible.
While speaking of the Expropriation Act, which is chapter 106 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, I should like to make particular reference to two cases which occurred locally but which have national implications, inasmuch as under the existing law the same thing can occur anywhere in Canada. But before I deal with these cases, Mr. Speaker, I should just like to tell the house that I was formerly an executive officer of a rural electrification scheme in Alberta, and as such it was my duty to invoke expropriation laws in that province. This I did according to law and justice. When this electrification line was constructed I had to get permission from certain farmers for the line to cross their land. Four farmers in the area did not agree.
I therefore went to court, for which provision had been made, and got authority to expropriate sufficient area to place seven or nine power poles-I forget the exact number now-on each quarter section, each half mile. The farmers received payment in advance of the poles being erected; but when the farmers finally wanted to receive the power they had to pay the money back. Nevertheless everyone was happy; there was no trouble.
However, Mr. Speaker, this is not always the case. My colleagues and I have taken cognizance of your letter of August 15, 1967 proposing that a special federal-provincial conference be held early next year to consider the possibility of giving Canada a constitutional Bill of rights providing especially a wider definition of and greater guarantees for the official languages.
Quebec has long been wishing that the rights of French in Canada be enlarged and that their observance be guaranteed by the constitution. Consequently, we can only rejoice at any initiative likely to produce such a result and I can assure you of the active participation of our government in the conference you propose.
However, I wish to draw to your attention that the changes that you seem to advocate will be difficult to implement unless the whole constitutional question is considered and resolved. Indeed, it is difficult to see how such a Bill of rights could be included in our constitution before the latter is repatriated. The unfortunate experience of the Fulton-Favreau formula has shown that such repatriation cannot be effected until agreement is reached on the outlines of constitutional reform.
I must add that even if it were possible to guarantee even more fully the rights of French under the constitution, the basic problem concerning Canada's future would still be far from being solved.
Our government deems it necessary to discuss a Bill of rights within the framework of a comprehensive study of our constitutional structures, rather than as a preliminary step to that study, as implied by your letter. Fortunately, the Confederation of tomorrow Conference which will be held in Toronto at
the end of the month, will give us the opportunity to undertake such a comprehensive study, thus enabling us to consider both questions at the same time and to make the necessary parallels.
Finally, I point out that, pursuant to its election platform, our government intends to include in the Quebec constitution a charter stipulating the fundamental rights and essential freedoms of man. As stated in your letter of February 10 last, the provinces do have an obvious interest in the matter.
Yours sincerely,
Daniel Johnson

My dear Prime Minister:
My colleagues and I have had an opportunity to consider carefully the contents of your letter of August 15 th in which you propose a conference early in 1968 to explore the possibility of establishing a constitutional Bill of Rights for Canada. We are much interested in such a conference and favor a date as early in January as possible.
It might be helpful if I indicated to you at this time our general thinking on this important matter. We agree fully with your observation that "the traditional rights and liberties of citizens are maintained at as high a level in Canada as in any country of the world." This fact, in our view, minimizes the practical need for a constitutional Bill of Rights in that it will do little more than confirm within the Constitution itself a fact of Canadian life that already exists and which is in little, if any, danger of being challenged.
The entrenchment of these unchallenged rights in the Constitution itself has a number of far-reaching implications which in our view require the most serious consideration. In a sense it means circumscribing the parliamentary and legislative powers of the federal and the provincial governments in that the constitutional Bill of Rights would supersede the present right of Parliament and legislatures to legislate in this field.
It is doubtful under present circumstances if unanimity could be obtained for the proposition that such an overriding provision should be inserted into the Constitution. There also is the question of whether such an addition to the Constitution should precede the adoption of an amending procedure.
It is a matter of sincere regret that the amending procedure agreed to unanimously by the federal and provincial governments and endorsed by most of the provincial legislatures, was rejected by Quebec which province thereby prevented its enactment.
Consideration also should be given to the fact that a constitutional Bill of Rights raises the danger of subversive groups challenging society's right to call their actions into question even when they obviously are designed
November 21, 1967

to undermine the foundations of our free and democratic way of life. The protection of society against flagrant abuses of fundamental rights is readily available as long as such rights gain their legal status through enactments of Parliament or the provincial legislatures. The situation would be very different if subversive elements could claim immunity from prosecution on the ground of an entrenched constitutional right.
In your letter you make specific reference to the question of language and the matter of language having an official status. In this matter it is our firm view that no attempt should be made to give official status to the French language by means of a constitutional provision other than the existing guarantee given to the Province of Quebec at the time of Confederation that French will be recognized, together with English, as an official language in Quebec.
The Government of Alberta does not accept the proposition that Confederation was a union of two races and two cultures. We hold the historic fact to be that Confederation was a union of provinces and that in the negotiations leading to Confederation the concept of the union being one of two races, two cultures and two languages was not a factor and certainly was in no sense a condition of the union.
The fallacious concept of relatively recent origin that Confederation was other than a union of provinces has done more to create divisions in Canada than it has to bring about national unity. The fact that almost one-third of Canadians are of neither English or French origin points up the serious disruptive long-range consequences which would result from designating French as a second national official language.
We, therefore, would be opposed to any amendment to the Constitution which would give further credence to a concept which we submit has no validity in history or in fact.
I make these observations at this time because I feel in all fairness you should know the considered opinion of the various provinces when assessing the desirability and possible value of the type of conference you have proposed.
Very sincerely yours,

My dear Premier:
You will recall that, in the course of the discussion I had with you and the Premiers of the other provinces following our lunch together at my house on July 5th, I said I would be writing to each of you about my proposal to hold a special Federal-Provincial Conference to consider the possibility of establishing a constitutional Bill of Rights for Canada. I had referred earlier to this possibility in the House of Commons on May 10th. I have now discussed the matter further with my Colleagues. We believe that a conference on a Bill of Rights could be a most constructive step in working toward the kind of modification in the constitution of Canada in the field of fundamental rights for all Canadians that seems clearly to be necessary as we move into the second century of our federal existence.
At the present time, the traditional rights and liberties of citizens are maintained at as high a level in Canada, I am sure, as in any country of the world. One cannot, however, but be aware of the fact that the formal guarantees of these rights and liberties are not endowed with the full constitutional sanction that seems to be desirable. The Canadian Bill of Rights passed in 1960 emphasizes the legal rights of citizens in respect of life, liberty, security of the person and so forth and also states a number of the basic political rights, including freedom of speech and the press, freedom of assembly and freedom of religion. It constituted as much protection in the matters it dealt with as could be given at the federal level without
constitutional amendment. However it is, of course, statutory and has therefore no force against the possibility of future action by Parliament. Obviously, as a federal statute it is not binding in any way on Provincial Legislatures.
The federal Bill of Rights of 1960 provides for equality of all citizens before the law and has other guarantees against discrimination. Most provinces also have anti-discrimination laws covering employment and other matters. These egalitarian rights are, as in the case of political and legal rights, not protected in any formal constitutional manner. So far as economic rights are concerned, few have been enunciated in any legislation in Canada and in the society of today it is worth considering whether they require some form of definition and guarantee.
Beyond the rights to which I have referred, which could, perhaps, be regarded as basic for any society of free people, we have to consider rights that are special to a country like Canada, which was founded on two distinct linguistic and cultural groups. To refer only to one matter, I think we have in the last few years become aware, in all parts of Canada, that language has a special importance as the instrument through which the cultural identity of a people is preserved and developed. We have not, I think, adequately considered whether, and, if so, what, constitutional consequences should flow from this fact. At the present time, the provisions in the British North America Act on language are extremely limited. I think we should consider whether we need to provide a broader definition and more extensive guarantees in respect of the official languages.
This brief outline of some of the matters that have to be considered will indicate how important and basic a discussion of a Bill of Rights could be for any future examination or our constitutional framework in a more general way. If we can achieve agreement on essential rights and on the way to define and protect them in all parts of Canada, I think we shall have made the most important single step that is required for the achievement of a satisfactory constitutional framework.
When we spoke on July 5th, I said I would suggest that the conference be either late in 1967 or early in 1968. On a matter as fundamental as this, it may be difficult to have adequate preparation in a matter of weeks. I am wondering, therefore, whether a meeting quite early in 1968 would meet with general convenience. It would be most helpful if you
November 21, 1967

could let me know whether a date in January or February would suit from your point of view and, if so, whether you have any particular preference.

Attorneys General. I would hope that those sessions would lead to a further definitive conference later in the year at which decisions on substance and method could be taken.
Yours sincerely,
(signed) Lester B. Pearson
The Honourable Louis J. Robichaud, Q.C., Premier of New Brunswick,
Fredericton, New Brunswick.
Wednesday, November 22, 1967
